hypotheses.text: The total worldwide published primary cohort defining SGSM3-related intellectual developmental disorder (OMIM #620401) across dedicated Mendelian discovery papers comprises fewer than 10 homozygous affected individuals, primarily split between an Ashkenazi Jewish founder cohort (Birnbaum et al.) and two affected siblings from a non-Ashkenazi kindred (Turkyilmaz et al.).
hypotheses.rationale: Evaluating exact penetrance and diagnostic discriminators requires establishing the denominator. Turkyilmaz et al. (2025) note that Birnbaum et al. first reported Ashkenazi Jewish families, while Turkyilmaz et al. report exactly two affected siblings with a homozygous stop-gain variant, indicating the total documented cohort across primary disease-definition papers is extremely small (N < 10).

evidence.text: Turkyilmaz et al. note: 'It was first reported by Birnbaum et al. that the SGSM3 gene might be associated with a Mendelian inherited disease in families of Ashkenazi Jews with clinical manifestations of intellectual disability (ID). In this study, a novel homozygous stop-gain (NM_015705.6: c.1576C>T: p.(Arg526Ter)) variation was detected in the SGSM3 gene in two siblings with short stature and ID findings. The report of two cases with bi-allelic LOF variants in the SGSM3 gene from different populations with similar clinical manifestations strengthens the potential of this gene...'

source.title: A Strong Candidate Gene for Nonsyndromic Intellectual Disability Phenotype: SGSM3
source.quote: In this study, a novel homozygous stop-gain (NM_015705.6: c.1576C>T: p.(Arg526Ter)) variation was detected in the SGSM3 gene in two siblings with short stature and ID findings. The report of two cases with bi-allelic LOF variants in the SGSM3 gene from different populations with similar clinical manifestations strengthens the potential of this gene as a candidate gene for the nonsyndromic ID phenotype.

hypotheses.text: Short stature (HP:0004322) is present in 2/2 (100%) individuals described in the Turkyilmaz et al. cohort but is absent or non-syndromic in the Ashkenazi Jewish founder cohort described by Birnbaum et al., distinguishing nonsyndromic intellectual disability presentations from syndromic presentations.
hypotheses.rationale: Turkyilmaz et al. describe their two cases specifically with 'short stature and ID findings' while referring to SGSM3 as a strong candidate for 'nonsyndromic intellectual disability phenotype'. Understanding whether short stature segregates consistently or was an incidental co-occurrence in that specific family will clarify whether short stature should be a primary clinical discriminator.

evidence.text: Turkyilmaz et al. report a homozygous stop-gain variation detected in SGSM3 in two siblings presenting with short stature and intellectual disability findings.

hypotheses.text: The Ashkenazi Jewish founder variant in SGSM3 reported by Birnbaum et al. accounts for greater than 70% of all currently known molecularly confirmed MRT84 patients worldwide.
hypotheses.rationale: PanelApp Australia flags SGSM3 with the tag 'founder' for intellectual developmental disorder autosomal recessive 84, and the discovery was initially made in Ashkenazi Jewish kindreds. Given that only two additional siblings have been formally published by Turkyilmaz et al., the founder allele represents the vast majority of the established denominator.

new_directions.question_text: What are the exact patient-by-patient clinical and dysmorphology features tabulated in Birnbaum et al. (2024) across the Ashkenazi Jewish founder kindreds?
new_directions.rationale: Birnbaum et al. is the primary discovery cohort establishing OMIM #620401; getting the exact numerator and denominator for cranial circumference, facial gestalt, speech milestone attainment, and brain MRI findings will determine whether MRT84 can be phenotypically recognized without sequencing.

new_directions.question_text: Did the Harripaul et al. (2021) consanguineous ASD trio cohort identify homozygous or compound heterozygous SGSM3 variants in patients, and what were their specific neurobehavioral findings?
new_directions.rationale: Harripaul et al. (2021) screened consanguineous ASD trios and explicitly identified candidate variants in SGSM3, which may expand the known clinical spectrum beyond classical ID to high-functioning autism spectrum presentations.
